newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke-under no political contraints on rates.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke-under no political contraints on rates.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the decision on UK interest rates is finely balanced and he was under no political pressure to leave rates on hold until the election, he told the Financial Times.

The interview reported that Clarke said while voters may not like higher mortgage rates, they also wanted assurance the recovery was sustainable. "I do no feel under any political contraints," he said.

Clarke said he was confident he would hit the 2.5 percent inflation target. "But it is like my ambitions on tax rates, it is like my ambitions on the balanced budget -- of course you set policy to hit them but you do so in a way that is consistent with the all-round information."
Other comments he made on the economy showed Clarke believes there was no risk of economic growth running out of control.
Consumer demand and house prices are picking up from very low levels, he said.

"People who say this has the feel of the 1980s about it should look at earnings -- at the complete contrast with the behaviour of British economy of the late 1980s in that earnings remain steady," he said.
The report said Clarke appeared to be happy to live with his differences with Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George.
The minutes of the December monetary meeting are due to be released at 0930 GMT and expected to show that George pressed for a rate rise and Clarke overruled him.
"I think people have got to get this thing in proportion. They need to have a grown-up debate. We are not in the world of flaming rows," Clarke said.

He did not mind if George gave speeches on the subject. Last week, George made a forthright speech in which he challenged Clarke's thinking in leaving rates on hold because of the pound's recent strength.
